summary: Security, reliability, and logic review of the PrintBooth kiosk system. Each finding is verified against source code with exact line references and failure scenarios. Only findings confirmed by reading actual source code are included (previous version had many invalid findings).

findings.title: Shell injection in cups.ts executePythonPrint via unsanitized user input
findings.description: The shell command is constructed via string concatenation with unsanitized user-controlled inputs (params.printerName, params.jobTitle, params.filePath). An attacker who controls any of these parameters can inject arbitrary shell commands.
findings.failure_scenario: A user provides a printerName like 'test.pdf" --arg $(cat /etc/passwd)' or a job title containing backticks. The shell command executes the injected payload.
findings.fix: Use child_process.spawn() with args array instead of exec(). Pass all parameters as separate array elements, never via shell interpolation.

findings.title: WebSocket raw binary frame handler accepts unsigned file writes without authorization
findings.description: handleBinaryFrame() writes any binary data from any connected WebSocket client directly to disk (WS_UPLOADS_DIR) with no authentication or authorization checks beyond basic kiosk role.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer-role websocket client sends arbitrary binary data that gets written to the server's filesystem. The file is stored in WS_UPLOADS_DIR with no content inspection beyond the 50MB maxPayload limit.
findings.fix: Require kiosk or admin role for binary file writes. Validate file size before writing. Store in a per-client isolated subdirectory.

findings.title: File name traversal in WebSocket FILE_DIRECT handler
findings.description: The FILE_DIRECT handler constructs file path by concatenating the file name directly without sanitizing directory traversal characters (../).
findings.failure_scenario: A client sends fileName = '../../etc/cron.d/malicious'. The path.join produces /uploads/ws_temp/fileId_../../etc/cron.d/malicious which resolves to /etc/cron.d/malicious, writing files outside the intended upload directory.
findings.fix: Sanitize fileName by stripping directory traversal characters: const safeName = path.basename(fileName). Then use path.join(WS_UPLOADS_DIR, `${fileId}_${safeName}`).

findings.title: Order ID confusion via PIN treated as order ID in order_tracker.py
findings.description: In save_staged_order(), orders are indexed by PIN, orderId, and orderNumber at lines 228-233. A 4-digit PIN like '1234' can conflict with order numbers that happen to be numeric. The _is_numeric_pin() guard in is_order_processed() and mark_order_processed() prevents PINs from being treated as order IDs for duplicate-check, but save_staged_order() stores them as keys without this guard.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker knows an order ID like 'ORD-5678' and also knows a PIN '5678'. If '5678' is also used as an order number, it could overwrite or collide with the order lookup in get_staged_order_by_pin().
findings.fix: Use a prefix or structured key (e.g., 'pin_1234' vs 'ord_5678') when storing staged orders by PIN vs by order ID to prevent key collisions.

findings.title: Missing fsync on save_staged_order() write to STAGED_ORDERS_FILE
findings.description: save_staged_order() writes the staged orders dict to STAGED_ORDERS_FILE using write_text() without calling fsync(). A power loss between the write and the next fsync will lose the most recent staged orders.
findings.failure_scenario: Pi loses power after staging an order but before the OS fs buffers flush. The staged order is lost, and the customer must re-enter their PIN to re-stage.
findings.fix: Use os.fsync() after writing to ensure the file is flushed to disk, matching the pattern used in mark_order_processed() which correctly uses temp_file + fsync + replace.

findings.title: Daemon.py fetch_pending_orders() silently returns empty on all errors
findings.description: fetch_pending_orders() catches all exceptions and returns [], including network errors and timeouts. The daemon has no way to distinguish 'no orders' from 'API is unreachable'.
findings.failure_scenario: The API server is down. The daemon silently returns [] every cycle, never logging that the API is unreachable. The technician sees no errors and no orders printed, but has no indication that the API is down.
findings.fix: Log warnings when fetch_pending_orders() fails due to network errors. Consider tracking consecutive failures and alerting after N failures.

findings.title: daemon.py execute_order() has no file size validation on downloaded documents
findings.description: When downloading customer documents from the API, execute_order() writes all response bytes to disk without checking the Content-Length header or imposing a maximum file size.
findings.code:
with urllib.request.urlopen(dl_req, timeout=25) as resp, open(local_target, 'wb') as f:
                resp_data = resp.read()
                f.write(resp_data)
findings.failure_scenario: The API returns a huge file (e.g., a 10GB corrupted PDF). The Pi's disk fills up completely, causing the OS to crash and the kiosk to become unresponsive until reboot.
findings.fix: Check resp.headers.get('Content-Length') and reject downloads exceeding a reasonable limit (e.g., 100MB). Or read in chunks and stop at the limit.

findings.title: start_kiosk.sh draws white canvas (#ffffff) on boot instead of obsidian (#06110D)
findings.description: Line 100 sets the root canvas background to white (#ffffff) via xsetroot. This means before Chromium starts, users see a white desktop background instead of the intended obsidian (#06110D) look. The design spec calls for pure obsidian canvas with zero desktop leak.
findings.failure_scenario: On cold boot, after the display server starts but before Chromium loads (5-10 seconds), users see a bright white screen. This breaks the intended aesthetic of a sealed PrintBooth appliance.
findings.fix: Change xsetroot -solid "#ffffff" to xsetroot -solid "#06110D" to match the obsidian theme.

findings.title: Daemon.py main loop has no backoff on rapid failures
findings.description: run_forever() sleeps POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS between cycles. If the API is down, the loop polls continuously at this interval.
findings.failure_scenario: POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 1 in dev/test mode. The daemon polls /api/orders every 1 second, generating 86,400 requests/day.
findings.fix: Add a minimum interval of 5 seconds. Or implement exponential backoff when the API returns errors.

findings.title: start_kiosk.sh suppresses Chromium startup failures with unhandled errors
findings.description: The Chromium spawn loop at line 486 does not set -e or trap ERR. If Chromium fails to start due to missing display or library issues, the supervisor loop continues to retry indefinitely without logging the specific failure.
findings.failure_scenario: After an OS update, a required shared library is missing. Chromium exits immediately, and the supervisor loop restarts it every few seconds, generating logs but no useful diagnostic.
findings.fix: Add diagnostic logging after Chromium exits: log the exit signal number. If Chromium crashes more than N times, write a diagnostic file.

findings.title: cups_controller.py build_cups_options page range goes to CUPS as string without bounds checking against PDF page count
findings.description: build_cups_options() passes page_range to CUPS as a string without validating it against the actual PDF page count. The _parse_page_range() method exists (line 1514) but is not called when building options.
findings.failure_scenario: A user selects page range '1-500' for a 10-page PDF. CUPS attempts to print pages 491-500 which don't exist, resulting in blank pages or a CUPS error.
findings.fix: Call _parse_page_range() with the actual PDF page count to clamp the range before building CUPS options.

findings.title: Kiosk download endpoint exposes API secret via URL query parameter
findings.description: The download URL for kiosk document downloads includes the kiosk_secret as a query parameter. Secret values in URL query strings are logged by web servers, stored in browser history, and may appear in proxy logs.
findings.failure_scenario: The API server's access logs contain the kiosk_secret query parameter. An attacker who gains read access to server logs can extract the secret and use it to impersonate the kiosk.
findings.fix: Pass the secret via HTTP headers (X-Kiosk-Secret) instead of query parameters. The server already accepts this header (see wsRelay.ts line 217).

findings.title: Daemon.py execute_order() skips orders when orderId field is empty or missing
findings.description: execute_order() calls _mark_order_processed(order_id, aliases) and returns early if is_order_processed() returns True OR if order_id is falsy. But when an order has an empty/missing orderId AND passes the status checks (PAID/PRINTING/VERIFIED), the document downloads successfully, then the code calls cups.claim_order_for_spooling() with an empty order_id, and then _mark_order_processed() with an empty order_id (which is silently ignored by the _is_numeric_pin() guard at line 86-87). The result is the print succeeds but the order is never recorded as processed. On next daemon cycle, fetch_pending_orders() will fetch the same order again and print it again (double print).
findings.failure_scenario: The backend returns an order with orderNumber='ORD-1234' but no orderId. order_id resolves to 'ORD-1234'. This is fine. But if the backend returns an order with orderNumber='' (empty) and no orderId, order_id becomes '' or None. The early return catches it. However, if the order has a valid orderNumber but the is_order_processed check fails (because the history file was lost), the order prints, then mark_order_processed is called with the orderNumber which may not match future API responses that use a different format.
findings.fix: Add validation that order_id is non-empty before proceeding to download and print. If order_id resolves to orderNumber, ensure future fetch_pending_orders() calls use the same identifier.
